messages.content:
Our world was once complete, and that which is complete bears no purpose. Locked in place, unshifting as it was uninteresting. A vast expanse that had been choked by time. Those who live now know not of what it means to suffocate. Not truly. When we die, our bodies reform, reintegrate into the world where they are needed most. There was nothing like that in these cold and desolate hills.

You could feel the grains forcing their way into your mouth, the unbearable weight from above stifling every attempt to force your way up for air. That beating, bleeding heart of humanity is only possible due to the unformed space we carry within ourselves. Room for air to enter, room for the gas we form to expel. There was no room like that. Not then. It rushed and rushed in. A ceaseless flow cascading down your throat, filling your lungs, filling your stomach, every orifice pierced until no part of your body, inside or out, could move.

How can a world create when it can't move? That is what it means to reach the end of a world. Unfettered uniformity. Chaos come to order. Creativity come to rigidity. There was no room for love or anger or sadness or hate. There was simply that which was.

From that, time was born again. A radiant font burst forth from the ground, as if it were perfectly natural. The very notion that this world had ever operated otherwise would be considered ridiculous were you to lay your eyes upon this magnificent sight. It was an endless stream, brimming with untapped potential. If you were to enter it, you would surely be consumed, carried away and born again into the ether of reality.

Man is not so foolish as to be run asunder by such a cataclysmic force. The fountain of energy was harnessed, for all that which can be imagined, from the foul and wicked to the beautiful and loving. It became the source of all that which made the wheels of this world turn. This force would be known by many names by many cultures. The arcane. The divine. Perhaps that which it is best known as would be magic, though that's not exactly accurate.

The miracles it performs are no mysterious force from beyond our world, they simply are our world, reshaped and molded to our desires. Just as we once choked on a world filled to the brim with itself, will we one day suffocate not from that which we have in excess, but rather from that which we so sorely lack? This magic thins every day, imperceptible as it might be to the naked eye. When it's gone, we can only hope that force which controls the course of our world is kind enough to turn back time and return that which fuels us.

This world may be comprised of many different nations, but there is one thing which is shared between all who call this planet their home. This world holds a vast ocean, stretching out beyond anywhere its inhabitants are capable of viewing with the naked eye. However, there is naught but water and its aquatic lifeforms waiting for them in these distant waves. No, there is only one landmass here on Turtima, and perhaps that is the only unshifting truth in its written history.

Pushed together and confined onto one continent, different nations have held disputes over resources and borders since as far back as our records go. Even in the modern age, it would be pointless to try to produce a definitive document detailing who controls what, and which people belong to whom. Wars over such details are being waged to this very day, and perhaps that conflict will never cease, so long as the scarcity of our world continues.

Though the landmass is vast, its continuous and unbroken nature leads to a single truth. Most of it is nigh uninhabitable by man. The coasts bear fruit, blessed by rainfall and vibrant ecosystems. Heading further in, you reach highly fertile soil for agriculture, while heading further out leads you to waters ideal for trade routes. On the other hand, in the center, far from the tides and moist atmosphere granted upon the circumference of this land, lies a vast desert.

Several kingdoms have fallen and risen along the exterior of this continent, while the desert settlements remain largely unincorporated and unaligned to larger political bodies. The extent of the interaction between larger nations and the communities inhabiting the desert is primarily during the establishment of occasional colonies when a profitable location for mining is found. Able-bodied members of the settlements are brought to the colonies, by trade or by force, and resources are shared with the visitors.

It has long been hoped that the desert may be used for transportation between nations on opposite sides of the landmass. Were this to come to fruition, one would no longer need to sail around the entire known world for the sake of trade or travel. Unfortunately, a sufficiently fast, comfortable, and dependable mode of transportation had not been developed. That is the very problem in which the greatest innovators of this world have set their minds to. This process has resulted in what may prove to be the most important invention in known history: the steam locomotive.

­
On the southern border of Turtima lies the country of Newark, led by its prime minister Aster Baldwin. Widely considered one of the two great political superpowers of the modern day, few would be surprised by how far its technological marvels stand above its contemporaries. Miracles spawning steel at a rapid rate, metal carriages that roll on their own, baskets that soar through the sky. All of this is made possible not through the magical myths of yore but of modern technology.

Even those inventions the world is familiar with are improved upon by in Newark. Boats powered by rotary devices rather than the wind, and, of course, firearms that are ever more capable of returning men to the very soil that granted us these devices. It is not all perfect in Newark, despite what Baldwin's men may try to present. Newark has little in the way of natural resources, and the reckless funding of innovative products has left the country with quite the debt. Within its borders are the minds which shall change the world, but it is from outside that the capital needed to do so lies.

Emperor Sunatra Layta from the empire of Yondova, situated at the very North of Turtima, has his eyes on the genius behind Newark's recent rapid progress. Yondova is a country of culture, making a fortune from exports of literature, tourism for its grand stage plays, and most of all from its music. To hear the hypnotizing tune spun by a Yondovan musician is considered by many a necessity in one's lifetime, and a luxury they will pay any price for. The instruments and techniques mastered within its Musical guild are trade secrets, as they are the key to Yondova remaining the second superpower of the modern age.

Unfortunate as it may be, the sheer distance from Yondova to the southern nations means that half of Turtima is all but cut off from ever hoping to hear the siren song of the finest Yondovan artists. Thus, when Layta heard news of a prototype vehicle that could allow direct passage across the continent, he decided that Yondova must control it. He began correspondence with Baldwin, offering to provide the necessary funds for the production of the first transcontinental railroad straight from one nation to the other.

Though Yondova's offer may appear to be mutually beneficial, centering both as crucial centers of trade from the northern and southern regions of Turtima, Newarkers are nothing if not skeptical. Though relations appear benevolent on both sides, in the world of politics, those who become complacent are those who fertilize the growth of their enemies first. Regardless, they were left with little choice.

The railroad has begun production, and the track has just reached a small village in the depths of the desert, a fact that reached the engineers far too late. As of now, the track is planned to cut straight through this settlement, and to tear it up and turn course earlier would be an unnecessary cost. Discussions have begun regarding the relocation of the village's population, but have been met quite forceful pushback. Though the villagers may be stubborn, they're not blind to the situation. Both Newark and Yondova are determined to get this railroad built, one way or another.
